newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.N. sends relief supplies to Afghan frontlines.
newsitem.headline: U.N. sends relief supplies to Afghan frontlines.

text.p: A U.N. aid coordinating agency said on Monday it had sent emergency relief for Afghans living in miserable conditions on battle frontlines, with children dying of cold and hunger in one area.

The U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Assistance to Afghanistan (UNOCHA) said in a statement in Islamabad that convoys carrying urgently needed supplies were heading for the country's frontline areas.
UNOCHA said in the statement that as many as four children were dying each day due to cold and hunger in Sang-i-Atash area in northwestern province of Badghis.

The Taleban Islamic militia is battling forces of former government commander Ahmad Shah Masood in the rugged Panjsher Valley north of Kabul and of his ally, Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum, in the northwest.
UNOCHA said one convoy left Kabul with plastic sheets, blankets, wheat flour, edible oil and winter clothing for about 8,000 people still living in towns north of the capital.

It said a U.N. mission to the area on Sunday found that 3,500 people remained in the town of Charikar, 1,750 in Istalif, 1,400 in Karabagh, 700 in Khalaka and 700 in Sri-i-Khuja. Most of them were too poor, old or sick to leave.
A U.N. official told reporters on Sunday that the Taleban had promised help in relief distribution and a return to normalcy in the area north of Kabul.

In western Afghanistan, a 25-truck U.N. convoy, carrying food, blankets and winter coats, set off from Herat for the remote northwestern province of Badghis, scene of the second frontline, the statement said.
Heavy fighting in Badghis over the past three months has led to the displacement of 40,000 to 50,000 people, but around 11,000 people are still in towns near the frontline, it said.

"Hundreds of other people are believed to have fled in smaller groups to the hills or trapped by the frontline, where they are understood to be in very poor condition," the agency said. There had been heavy snowfalls in the area and temperatures had fallen to as low as -10 degrees Celsius.

It said monitors of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees had estimated that 90,000 people displaced by fighting, forced evacuations and other military activities had entered Kabul over the past three weeks.

The Taleban, which has taken control of about two-thirds of the war-ravaged nation in two years since the movement was born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan, is committed to bringing its stern version of Islam's Sharia law to the whole country.
